newsitem.title: USA: Perry says U.S. troops won't patrol Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Perry says U.S. troops won't patrol Hebron.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's suggestion that U.S. troops could help patrol the West Bank city of Hebron is not being considered as a way of resolving Israeli-Palestinian differences, Defence Secretary William Perry said on Tuesday.
"This has been proposed before and it is not under active consideration," he said before a meeting with Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai.

U.S. officials, meanwhile, played down prospects of an imminent agreement between Israel and the Palestinians on an Israeli redeployment in Hebron, despite optimistic statements from some Israeli officials.

Arafat said in Jericho, where he was hosting Jordan's King Hussein, that he was ready to have U.S. troops join an international force to guard the 400 Jewish settlers in Hebron, a city of 100,000 Arabs, to resolve the dispute.

"I told them, okay, if you don't trust the joint mobile units and you don't trust your soldiers or our soldiers, okay, why not call upon the international presence with the participation of the American army?" Arafat said.
Israel agreed last year to pull back its troops in Hebron but Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he wants provisions to safeguard the Jewish settlers.

Netanyahu's media adviser, David Bar-Illan, said Arafat's proposal "may actually cause the deaths of American soldiers in this area and I doubt very much whether bringing home American troops to America in body bags is going to ... further ... the peace process."
Mordechai made no comment on the idea of an international force but said Israel intended to redeploy its troops in Hebron when agreement was reached on the settlers' security.
"I hope in a very short time we will have agreement with the Palestinian Authority and when we have agreement in very short time we can redeploy in Hebron," he said.

Arafat, however, said in Jericho on Tuesday there had been no progress in negotiations on the Hebron redeployment, which are being mediated by U.S. special Middle East coordinator Dennis Ross. U.S. officials also spoke of serious differences.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said that although "some progress" had occurred, "there's been much too much talk in the press of some kind of immediate, positive outcome here."

"Following my conversation with Dennis and my conversation with Secretary (of State Warren) Christopher just now, substantial differences remain between Israel and the Palestinians," he told a news briefing.

Although Burns blamed the media for the optimism, other U.S. officials made clear they believed Israeli officials were exaggerating the progress. "Despite what the Israelis are saying, there's been no breakthrough in the talks," one said.
